{{Short description|Philosophical position regarding the role of psychology}}
{{about|the family of philosophical positions|the subfield of philosophical study|Philosophy of psychology}}

'''Psychologism''' (or '''logical psychologism''') is a family of [[philosophical]] positions, according to which [[logical law]]s, truths, or principles are grounded in, [[Reductionism|reducible]] to, or explained by [[psychological]] facts, laws, or processes.

The term was coined by [[Johann Eduard Erdmann]] as ''Psychologismus'', being translated into English as ''psychologism''.<ref name="SEoP">''[[Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]'', [http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/psychologism/ Psychologism].</ref><ref>[[Martin Kusch|Kusch, M.]], ''Psychologism: The Sociology of Philosophical Knowledge'' (London & New York: [[Routledge]], 1995), [https://books.google.com/books?id=JJuIAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA101&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q&f=false p. 101].</ref>

== Definition ==
The ''[[Oxford English Dictionary]]'' defines ''psychologism'' as: "The view or doctrine that a theory of psychology or ideas forms the basis of an account of metaphysics, epistemology, or meaning; (sometimes) spec. the explanation or derivation of mathematical or logical laws in terms of psychological facts."<ref>''Oxford English Dictionary''.</ref> Psychologism in [[epistemology]], the idea that its problems "can be solved satisfactorily by the psychological study of the development of mental processes", was argued in [[John Locke]]'s ''[[An Essay Concerning Human Understanding]]'' (1690).<ref>''[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]'', Psychologism.</ref>

Other forms of psychologism are logical psychologism and mathematical psychologism. Logical psychologism is a position in [[logic]] (or the [[philosophy of logic]]) according to which [[Classical logic|logical laws]] and [[mathematics|mathematical]] laws are grounded in, derived from, explained or exhausted by psychological facts or laws. Psychologism in the [[philosophy of mathematics]] is the position that mathematical concepts and/or truths are grounded in, derived from or explained by psychological facts or laws.<ref>[[Shaun Gallagher|Gallagher, S.]], ''Phenomenology'' ([[New York City|New York]]: [[Palgrave Macmillan]], 2012), [https://books.google.com/books?id=c7sYDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA20&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q&f=false p. 20].</ref>

== Viewpoints ==
[[John Stuart Mill]] was accused by [[Edmund Husserl]] of being an advocate of a type of logical psychologism, although this may not have been the case.<ref>Skorupski, J. M., [https://books.google.com/books?id=ghesAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA127&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q&f=false ''Mill (Arguments of the Philosophers)''], Routledge, 2010, pp. 127-128.</ref> So were many nineteenth-century German philosophers such as [[Christoph von Sigwart]], [[Benno Erdmann]],  [[Theodor Lipps]], [[Gerardus Heymans]], [[Wilhelm Jerusalem]], and [[Theodor Elsenhans]],<ref name=SEP>{{cite web |last1=Kusch |first1=Martin |title='3. Examples of Psychologistic Reasoning' in ''Psychologism'' |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/psychologism/#ExaPsyRea |website=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |publisher=The Metaphysics Research Lab |access-date=3 January 2019 |date=Winter 2015}}</ref> as well as a number of psychologists, past and present (e.g., [[Wilhelm Wundt]]<ref name=SEP/> and [[Gustave Le Bon]]).<ref>[[Jerzy Szacki|Szacki, J.]], ''History of Sociological Thought'', [[Greenwood Publishing Group|Greenwood Press]], 1979, p. 252.</ref>

Psychologism was notably criticized by [[Gottlob Frege]] in his [[anti-psychologism|anti-psychologistic]] work ''[[The Foundations of Arithmetic]]'', and many of his works and essays, including his review of Husserl's ''[[Philosophy of Arithmetic]]''.<ref>Haddock, G. E. R., ''A Critical Introduction to the Philosophy of Gottlob Frege'' ([[London]] and [[New York City|New York]]: [[Routledge]], 2006), [https://books.google.com/books?id=wsi1CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA110&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q&f=false p. 110].</ref> Husserl, in the first volume of his ''[[Logical Investigations (Husserl)|Logical Investigations]]'', called "The Prolegomena of Pure Logic", criticized psychologism thoroughly and sought to distance himself from it. Frege's arguments were largely ignored, while Husserl's were widely discussed.<ref name="SEoP" />

In "Psychologism and Behaviorism", [[Ned Block]] describes psychologism in the [[philosophy of mind]] as the view that "whether behavior is intelligent behavior depends on the character of the internal information processing that produces it." This is in contrast to a behavioral view which would state that intelligence can be ascribed to a being solely via observing its behavior. This latter type of behavioral view is strongly associated with the [[Turing test]].<ref>{{Citation
 | last = Block | first =  Ned | author-link = Ned Block
